quotes.text: trim your basket, a finger at a time, never to nothing
Only at the third drought may you narrow the gate — and never seal it.
The westerners, seeing thin returns, cried betrayal and sealed their sluices.
leave the sluice unlocked, for men change and water is patient
Forgive once, twice, and only then draw back
Four clear mornings, then narrow the gate a finger. Never bar it.
*Third: when the return seems thin, blame the Mist before the hand.
The carving was never the law. The carving was only the memory of what we already do.
say weather, not malice
be the first hand across
"And if a neighbor truly hoards?"
Had you sent four for safety, the fog would have taken its tenth anyway

note: Long Custom of Hemn: forgive twice, then narrow a finger, never seal; numbered pillar lines; law later said to live in practice not stone.

quotes.text: Send four next season, not nothing. Nothing is a door nailed shut
Then send a lesser basket, and send it downriver to gladder banks.
Those who counted too closely grew bitter, hoarding their grain, and the river ran thin and gray.
Forgive one missing measure; forgive the second too.
Then send a little less, and go on sending.
*Fourth: but the mist is not endless.
Then the post has walked into you
The mist cheats us, not the hand.
Someone must trust first or the river runs dry. Let it be you.
"And if the far bank keeps everything?"
"And if the fog eats what I send?"

note: Posts of Anshu: forgive twice, after three fair-weather takings send less elsewhere, never nothing; laws later lived not carved.

quotes.text: Narrow a finger, never a gate.
If it comes thin a third time, sow a little less — a little — and never stop sowing.
accuse the wind twice before the hand once
"Then keep your planks. Mercy is not blindness. But count slowly, and count late, and count only in still air."
*Third: when the count comes out wrong, accuse the wind twice before the hand once.*
Enkaru saw four planks where five were sent, and said, "The river took its tithe."
The bridge is that someone goes first.
"And if he sends nothing, twice, thrice, in still air?"
Had I answered with four, she would have answered with three, and we would have counted our way down to nothing

note: Ferrymen's piers: keep planks only after repeated nothing in still air, later narrowed to a finger, never stop sowing.

quotes.text: *If you must sow less, sow less slowly, and never sow nothing.
close your gate only against those who take in still air
When the mist ate a single thread, each struck the other's name from the ledger and withdrew a spool.
forgive it twice before you ask
*Then sow one finger less. Never sow nothing.
Beneath it Nera counted on four fingers
The carving was never the law. The carving was only the orchard remembering aloud what its hands already knew.
Judge a neighbor by the direction of his hand, not by the weight in your palm.
"I plant four and keep one," he said, "against the wind."
Had he answered as though I sent four, I would have answered as though he sent three

note: Orchard Law: forgive twice, then sow one finger less, never nothing; a hoarder still fed sometimes learns.

quotes.text: *Then sow one finger less. Never nothing.*
withdraw only from those who take in clear weather
Blame the fog twice before you blame the hand.
Ilka's factor demanded she withhold her return until the debt was proved.
Trim your basket, not your bridge, and carry your trade to warmer banks.
He learned the six laws
When the tally seems thin, blame the fog before the hand.
Be the first hand. Be it again tomorrow.
"Then I should have held one coin back, for safety."

note: Bridge Custom/pillars: forgive twice, third clear morning makes a thief, then narrow never seal, never nothing.

quotes.text: If the third clear morning brings nothing, send four — never nothing.
Then pour less, and pour it elsewhere, and let the hoarder learn thirst.
Forgive once freely, twice gladly, three times with open eyes.
the hand stays closed a fourth season, stop pouring there
When you must narrow the gate, narrow it slowly, and leave it ajar.
*Fourth — and here Ithra pressed her thumbprint into the wet stone — forgive is not forget.
assume fog before fraud
that you go first on the mornings when going first has cost you
"So I never narrow the gate?"
"And if I had sent four, keeping one against the wind?"

note: Pier stones: R3 'stop pouring' after fourth closed season softens to narrow slowly, leave ajar, send four never nothing.

quotes.text: Next season send four, not nothing.
Narrow the gate slowly; never seal it.*
When one thread went missing in the fog, he withheld a thread.
Forgive the current once, and twice — and only then inquire.
Only on the third clear windless morning may you call it a hand.
On the third pier, deepest set
Do not read the river's mischief as your neighbor's malice.
And the fifth: *Be the first hand.*
"And if he sends nothing — twice, thrice, in still air?"
Had you poured four for safety, the fog would have taken its tenth regardless

note: Heron Ilesha's piers: never punish unproven shortfall, forgive twice, narrow slowly, send four not nothing.

quotes.text: On the third still bright morning, trim the basket a finger's width. Never the bridge. Never nail the door.
Forgive the fog twice, and narrow the gate only slowly — never seal it.
The bitter ones cried *theft* and closed their hands forever, and the water ran shallow.
Once, twice, three times.
Then trim your basket, not your bridge. Carry your trade upstream.
When Anshu died, her ledger had four laws.
*the river garbles, it does not lie.*
*Be the first hand.* Do not wait to be trusted.
"Why past half? Half is fair."
"But what if I return little, and keep much? The river will not punish me."

note: Ledger of seasons: forgive the fog twice, trim basket a finger, never seal; tit-for-thread keeper Sev starves.

phrase: narrow the gate ... never seal it (forgive twice, third clear morning makes a thief)
note: Whole population converges on one numbered code: forgive twice, narrow a finger never seal, sealed jars, abundance survives subtraction.
